Gulf of Mexico well interventions: the life of a well, then the work by water depth

A Gulf of Mexico development well lives about 23.0 years from first spud to permanent abandonment (median of 16,860 abandoned wells). Heavy, rig-based work comes early in that life and light wireline and coiled-tubing work later. In 2025, BSEE approved 765 interventions and 2,610 abandonments; per standing well, interventions are seven times as frequent in water deeper than 1,500 m as on the shelf (38.7 against 5.5 approvals per 100 wells).

Revision 3, 13 November 2026. Data: BSEE raw well data, files of 13 November 2026. Read the full study.

1. Why interventions matter

A well intervention is any job that goes back into a completed well to keep it working. The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) describes it this way in its Gulf of Mexico environmental study: completed and producing wells "may require periodic reentry that is designed to maintain or restore a desired flow rate", and the same work is used to test another reservoir zone, recomplete to it, or plug part of the well (BOEM 2016-018, section 3.1.3.5, p. 3-37). The study expects a producing well to have "seven workovers or other well activities during its lifetime" (p. 3-38).

Light and heavy. A light intervention works through the well's existing tubing with wireline or coiled tubing, from the platform, a liftboat or a vessel, without a rig. A heavy intervention brings in a rig or a hydraulic workover unit that can pull the tubing out of the well. On a subsea well, a workover traditionally "require[s] that a rig be moved on location" (BOEM, p. 3-37); purpose-built intervention vessels that run wireline or coiled tubing are "very cost effective in decommissioning subsea wells compared to using a drilling rig" (BSEE TAP-738, 2015, p. 5-21).

What it costs and saves. Most jobs take days, not months: the Gulf median is 7 days, within a range of 1 day to several months (BOEM, p. 3-37). The day rate is set by what has to be brought to the well. In the study's cost cases (2015 dollars), a rigless spread on a shelf platform costs about USD 64,530 a day and a light well-work job USD 0.53 to 0.98 million; a subsea well that needs a drillship or semisubmersible costs about USD 674,600 a day and USD 4.7 to 9.4 million (TAP-738, Table 8-2, p. 8-12, and p. 8-18; the cost method is in Appendix B). Choosing the lighter route saves rig days: a typical deepwater intervention takes 12 to 15 days with a rig against eight to 10 days with a vessel-deployed wireline system (TAP-738, p. 6-9). An intervention also keeps an existing well producing, which is the reason operators do one.

This article follows the wells first: how long a Gulf well lasts and what happens to it on the way (section 2). It then counts the interventions by water depth (section 3) and prices them by access type (section 4).

2. The life of a Gulf of Mexico well

BSEE's borehole file lists every well drilled in the Gulf, with its spud date, its sidetracks and bypasses, and the date each bore was permanently abandoned. Its permit-to-modify file lists every approved intervention and abandonment from 2005 on. Together they give each well a life story. Of the 37,512 Gulf wells with a spud date, 30,737 are permanently abandoned and 6,775 still stand.

  • Exploration wells have short lives: 8,583 of the 13,537 abandoned exploration wells were plugged within a year of spud (median 0.2 years).
  • Development wells that have been abandoned lived a median 23.0 years, the middle half between 11.3 and 35.3 years. The 5,570 development wells still standing are a median 42.0 years old.

The life story of a development well

A development well is drilled, and 36% of those drilled since 2005 have been sidetracked or bypassed, usually early (median 1.6 years after spud). Read across today's wells (Figure 2, right), heavy work with a rig or workover unit comes next, at a median age of 13.3 years; 59% of development wells drilled since 2005 have had at least one heavy intervention approved. Light wireline and coiled-tubing work follows as the well ages, at a median 24.1 years. Temporary abandonment comes at a median 32.3 years and permanent abandonment at 33.0 years. Development wells drilled since 2005 have had 4.2 intervention approvals each so far, against BOEM's expectation of seven workovers or other well activities in a lifetime; the ones still standing are a median 14.4 years old. An exploration well's story is short: two in three of those drilled since 2005 are already permanently abandoned, most within a year of spud, and its heavy work comes early (median age 4.8 years).

3. Interventions by water depth

In 2025, BSEE approved 765 interventions (well work) and 2,610 abandonments, 3,375 approvals in all. By water depth, the interventions were under 100 m: 316; 100 to 500 m: 99; 500 to 1,500 m: 185; 1,500 m and deeper: 165. The abandonments were 1,060 temporary, 1,387 permanent and 163 of unstated type. Three quarters of the abandonment approvals (1,963 of 2,610) were for wells in less than 100 m of water.

What the rate means

Figure 4 asks how often a standing well gets an approval in a year. A rate of 38.7 at 1,500 m and deeper in 2025 means about 0.4 intervention approvals for every standing deepwater well; 5.5 on the shelf means about one for every 18 standing shelf wells. The rate takes out the shrinking number of wells: 16,124 wells stood on 1 January 2005 and 7,636 on 1 January 2025.

  • Is intervention going up or down? Per standing well, it held in a narrow band for many years and has been lower since 2023. Across all depths, intervention approvals ran at 11.9 to 14.8 per 100 standing wells a year from 2006 to 2019, and at 9.4 to 10.5 from 2023 to 2025. The count fell further, from 2,099 in 2006 to 765 in 2025, mostly because there are fewer wells. Part of the recent step down is the coding change in note 2 of Figure 3.
  • Light or heavy? From 2014, at least three in four intervention approvals name a unit that can be classified (82% in 2025). Since then light work has run at 5.4 to 8.5 approvals per 100 standing wells a year and heavy work at 2.5 to 4.8. Light work averaged 7.6 in 2014-2019 and 5.6 in 2023-2025; heavy work averaged 3.8 and 2.8. Light work is about twice as frequent as heavy work, and both are lower in the last three years than in 2014-2019.
  • Deeper water, more work per well. In 2025 the intervention rate rises with depth (under 100 m: 5.5; 100 to 500 m: 11.2; 500 to 1,500 m: 32.6; 1,500 m and deeper: 38.7). Deepwater wells are fewer and more often subsea, and the operators' own estimates put the job at a median 14 days there against 3 on the shelf.
  • Abandonment ran at 34.2 approvals per 100 standing wells in 2025, against 10.0 for interventions. Abandonment is counted here and studied in the next article.

4. Cost per intervention, by access type

Cost follows how the well is reached, not depth alone. A dry-tree platform well can be worked from a rigless spread or casing jacks; a subsea well needs a vessel, a drillship or a semisubmersible. Figure 6 gives low, base and high cases per event in 2015 dollars from the BSEE and BOEM cost studies; the method and every source page are in Appendix B.

5. Abandonment

Abandonment approvals appear in this article only as counts and rates. The next article covers abandonment, temporary and permanent, in the same depth: why wells are left temporarily abandoned, how long they stay that way, and what permanent abandonment costs.

Appendix A. Counting rules

  1. Wells and life. One well is one API10 number in BSEE's borehole file, region G, with cancelled bores removed. A well starts at the earliest spud date of its bores. It ends when every bore that is not superseded (status ST or BP) is permanently abandoned (PA) with a date; the end is the latest of those dates. Otherwise it stands at 13 November 2026. Development (D) and exploration (E) follow the well type of the original hole (suffix ST00BP00).
  2. Drilling. Each bore with a spud date: the original hole and each sidetrack or bypass. Permits that prepare new hole (PLUGBACK, sidetrack, bypass or deepen) are excluded from the permit counts so that drilling is not counted twice.
  3. Permits. One approved permit to modify (one submission ID) is one event. WORKOVER, ENHANCE, COMP with ZONE, OTHER, INFORM and UTIL are interventions (well work). ABANDON with PERMABAN is permanent abandonment, else with TEMPABAN temporary abandonment, else of unstated type. COMP without ZONE (initial completion) is excluded. Approvals from 2005 to 13 November 2026 are counted; the feed begins part-way through 2004.
  4. Light or heavy. From the unit type the permit names (rig ID joined to the regulator's rig lookup). Light: wireline (WL), coiled tubing (CT), intervention vessel (WI), liftboat (LB), recorded non-rig operation (NR). Heavy: hydraulic workover or snubbing unit (HW, SB), platform rig (PF), jack-up rig (JU), drillship or semisubmersible (DS, SS, SD). Not classified: no unit named, or another type (barge, submersible, unmatched). These groups keep the unit categories of the permit counts, except that the combined "liftboat / jack-up" category is divided by its two source codes. Mapping: intervention_weight_mapping.csv.
  5. Water depth is the well's depth in feet times 0.3048, in four bands: under 100 m, 100 to 500 m, 500 to 1,500 m, and 1,500 m and deeper.
  6. Standing wells on 1 January use the same start and end rule as item 1.

Appendix B. Cost method

Spread scenarios multiply a published day rate by low, base and high durations and add mobilisation: rigless platform spread USD 64,530 a day (derived from TAP-738, Table 8-2, p. 8-12), casing jacks USD 68,424 a day (Table 8-3, p. 8-14), drillship or semisubmersible USD 674,600 a day (p. 8-18). Well-work durations are 7, 10.5 and 14 days (BOEM 2016-018 p. 3-37 median; one to two weeks from the BOEM Alaska update, 2012, p. 108). The deepwater dry-tree abandonment row is TAP-738's published per-well total (Table 8-4, p. 8-15). Costs are 2015 dollars, not escalated, and are scenarios, not bids. The full table, every input and its source page are in the full study (cost_table.csv).

Appendix C. Reusable prompt

This prompt rebuilds the life of every Gulf of Mexico well and the intervention counts from BSEE's public raw data, and adapts them to your own field or depth range. To have a study of your own wells done for you instead, see below.

What you need to run this

  • Data required: BSEE raw data, BoreholeRawData.zip and eWellAPMRawData.zip (and eWellEORRawData.zip and eWellWARRawData.zip for the cross-checks), from data.bsee.gov.
  • Data required to adapt: a list of API numbers, or a lease, area or depth range.
  • Paid or behind an account: nothing.
  • Changes over time: BSEE refreshes the files daily, so a new download gives slightly different recent counts.

Reproduce the published result

Using the worldenergydata repository at commit 2c9dcd0a33a7830f0fe4143aedec49988bb5b6bc, folder examples/bsee/interventions_by_depth:
download the four BSEE archives with download_data.py --snapshot 2026-11-13
(or use a later snapshot and expect small changes in recent years), then run
count_interventions.py, well_life_cycle.py, build_cost_basis.py, estimate_costs.py,
plot_charts.py, plot_life_cycle.py and build_article.py. Check that
output/life_cycle_reconciliation.csv shows the same published and counted totals,
and that 2025 gives 765 intervention and 2,610 abandonment approvals.

Adapt it to your project

Filter the borehole and permit tables to your wells before the life-cycle step.
Report, per well: life in years, bores drilled, light and heavy interventions,
temporary and permanent abandonment approvals, with the counting rules of Appendix A.
Keep approvals separate from completed jobs, and state the unit rule you use.

Data set: BSEE Data Center raw well data (public), files of 13 November 2026.
